title: Dry-run: choosing a realtime transport
intro: About 5 minutes. The four options look interchangeable in a slide, but the code makes the cost of each one concrete.

steps.title: Polling — simplest, and wasteful by construction
steps.explain: A fixed-interval request regardless of whether anything changed. Cheap to build, but latency is bounded by the interval and most requests return nothing — the waste is the whole point to call out.

steps.title: Long polling — same request shape, server holds it open
steps.explain: The server delays its response until there's data or a timeout, so a response almost always carries something. It's a real improvement with zero new infrastructure, which is why it's often the answer for 'realtime without websockets.'
steps.saysOutLoud: Long polling gets most of the latency win of a push transport with none of the new infra.

steps.title: Server-Sent Events — one connection, server pushes freely
steps.explain: SSE is a single long-lived HTTP connection the server writes to whenever it wants, with automatic reconnect built into the browser API. The catch is it's one-directional — the client still needs a normal request to send anything back.

steps.title: WebSocket — the only option that's bidirectional and low-latency
steps.explain: Full duplex over one persistent connection, no per-message HTTP overhead. This is the right call when the client also needs to send frequently — chat, collaborative editing — not just receive.

steps.title: Whichever you pick, the connection is a stateful resource
steps.explain: Long polling, SSE, and WebSocket all tie a client to one specific server process for the connection's lifetime, unlike stateless request/response. That server needs a registry so other backend processes can find and push to a given connection — the same registry pattern chat systems use.

steps.title: Reconnects need jittered backoff, not a fixed retry
steps.explain: A deploy or brief outage drops every open connection at once. If every client retries on the same fixed delay, they all reconnect simultaneously and can knock the recovering server back over — the fix is the same jittered exponential backoff used anywhere else clients retry en masse.

closing: If they ask for a one-line answer: default to long polling unless the client also needs to push frequently, in which case it's a WebSocket — SSE is the middle case when the server pushes a lot and the client barely talks back.
